question: Tell me about a time change kept rewriting the goal. How did you keep the team focused?
competency: Be decisive in ambiguity and change
principle: Be decisive in ambiguity and change

raiseTranscript.text: On my first project the PM kept shifting priorities every sprint because of new stakeholder input. I started writing a one-page change log each week and brought it to my manager for a quick sync.
What did you do when the team started losing momentum?
I asked each person to pick one task they could finish that week and we reviewed it in standup. We shipped two small features instead of the original big one.
How did you feel about the constant changes?
It was frustrating at first, but my manager told me to treat it as data so I started tracking how often things moved.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time change kept rewriting the goal. How did you keep the team focused?
Role: new grad on first feature team; situation: weekly priority flips from stakeholders
Actions: created weekly change log, synced with manager, broke work into one-week wins
Outcome: shipped two small features; team stayed in standup
Quote: "My manager told me to treat it as data"
Follow-up: How did you feel about the constant changes? → Started tracking frequency
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The candidate owned a small but repeatable process for handling goal churn instead of waiting for direction. The change log and weekly manager sync show coachability and local ownership. The quote about treating shifts as data indicates early learning agility. Biggest gap is that impact stayed inside one team and one manager relationship.

lowerTranscript.text: The requirements changed three times in a month and I just kept re-planning my tasks.
How did the rest of the team react?
They were confused too but we all waited for the PM to decide. I finished my part late.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time change kept rewriting the goal. How did you keep the team focused?
Role: new grad; situation: monthly requirement churn
Actions: kept re-planning personal tasks and waited for PM
Outcome: delivered late; team stayed confused
Quote: "We all waited for the PM to decide"
Follow-up: How did the rest of the team react? → No proactive steps taken
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. The candidate treated goal changes as something to endure rather than manage, showing limited ownership. Waiting for the PM to decide and delivering late indicates weak local agency. No evidence of asking for help or creating any visibility for the team. Biggest gap is absence of even small proactive steps.

raiseTranscript.text: Our cross-team migration got hit by three org reorgs in six months. I started running a bi-weekly "goal reset" meeting with the three tech leads and we published a shared risk register.
What metrics did you use to keep people aligned?
We tracked migration completion rate and on-call load per team. When the goal moved again we cut the scope to the top two services and moved the rest to the next quarter.
How did you handle pushback from one of the teams?
I asked their lead to bring their data to the reset meeting so the decision was visible instead of top-down.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time change kept rewriting the goal. How did you keep the team focused?
Role: senior on platform migration; situation: three reorgs in six months
Actions: ran bi-weekly goal reset with tech leads, published risk register, used completion and on-call metrics
Outcome: cut scope to top two services; decision made visible
Quote: "I asked their lead to bring their data to the reset meeting"
Follow-up: What metrics did you use? → Completion rate and on-call load; Follow-up: How did you handle pushback? → Made decision visible
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. The candidate used a repeatable reset ritual and visible metrics to drive cross-team decisions without authority. Cutting scope based on data shows decisive trade-off making. Involving the dissenting team lead in the meeting demonstrates influence without authority. Biggest strength is turning repeated ambiguity into a process others could follow.

lowerTranscript.text: I tried to keep the original plan alive by working extra hours and updating the roadmap every time leadership changed direction.
Did other teams adopt your updates?
Not really. One team just ignored the new dates and we missed the migration deadline.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time change kept rewriting the goal. How did you keep the team focused?
Role: senior on migration; situation: repeated leadership direction changes
Actions: worked extra hours and updated roadmap alone
Outcome: one team ignored dates; missed deadline
Quote: "One team just ignored the new dates"
Follow-up: Did other teams adopt your updates? → No cross-team alignment achieved
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. The candidate relied on personal heroics and solo roadmap updates instead of creating shared mechanisms. Missing the deadline after repeated changes shows lack of influence without authority. No metrics or visible decision process was introduced. Biggest gap is absence of any leverage beyond individual effort.

raiseTranscript.text: After the acquisition the product direction flipped twice in a quarter. I created a two-page decision framework with the CEO and used it to kill two initiatives and double down on the integration path.
What was the long-term signal you protected?
We kept the metric of active enterprise customers and showed that the new direction would drop it by 30 percent in year two.
How did you handle the teams whose work was deprioritized?
I met with each director, explained the framework, and gave them a 60-day runway to find new homes for their people inside the combined org.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time change kept rewriting the goal. How did you keep the team focused?
Role: exec post-acquisition; situation: two direction flips in one quarter
Actions: built decision framework with CEO, used customer metric to kill initiatives, gave 60-day runway to directors
Outcome: protected enterprise customer metric; people moved inside org
Quote: "I gave them a 60-day runway to find new homes for their people"
Follow-up: What was the long-term signal? → Active enterprise customers; Follow-up: How did you handle deprioritized teams? → 60-day runway
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. The candidate made visible strategic trade-offs using a shared framework and protected a multi-year customer metric. Giving directors a 60-day runway shows long-term thinking about org leverage rather than short-term heroics. The decision to kill initiatives based on quantified impact demonstrates decisive judgment under high ambiguity. Biggest strength is turning repeated goal changes into a durable decision system.

lowerTranscript.text: I kept communicating the latest direction in all-hands and asked teams to stay flexible.
What happened to the original roadmap commitments?
We slipped most of them and lost two key engineering leads who left because priorities kept moving.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time change kept rewriting the goal. How did you keep the team focused?

Outcome: slipped commitments; lost two engineering leads
Follow-up: What happened to the original roadmap commitments? → Attrition and missed dates
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. The candidate relied on broadcast communication without creating decision mechanisms or trade-off visibility. Biggest gap is absence of any durable process that outlasted the ambiguity.
